evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: Nomascus is the second-most speciose genus of gibbons (family Hylobatidae).

evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: Originally, this genus was a subgenus of "Hylobates", and all individuals were considered one species, "Hylobates concolor".

evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: Species within "Nomascus" are characterized by 52 chromosomes.

evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: Some species are all black, some are light with a distinct black tuft of crown fur, and some have distinct, light-colored cheek patches.

evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: "Nomascus" is found from southern China (Yunnan) to southern Vietnam, and also on Hainan Island.

evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: One species, "Nomascus nasutus," has been deemed "the most critically endangered ape species in the world".

evidence.title: Nomascus
evidence.text: All species in this genus are endangered or critically endangered.

evidence.title: Pseudopontia
evidence.text: Pseudopontia is a genus of butterflies found only in wet forests of tropical Africa.

evidence.title: Pseudopontia
evidence.text: It is the only genus in the subfamily Pseudopontiinae.

evidence.title: Pseudopontia
evidence.text: It was traditionally thought to contain only one species (monotypic), "Pseudopontia paradoxa".

evidence.title: Pseudopontia
evidence.text: However, a recent study showed there are at least five species of "Pseudopontia" which can be distinguished genetically and by details of wing veins.

evidence.title: Pseudopontia
evidence.text: Each is found primarily in a different part of Africa, though several of the species have overlapping geographic distributions.

evidence.title: Megacheira
evidence.text: Megacheira ("Great Hands") is an extinct class of predatory arthropods that possessed a pair of short enlarged appendages (the source of the class' name).

evidence.title: Megacheira
evidence.text: They strongly resemble early chelicerates.

evidence.title: Megacheira
evidence.text: Most of them were found in marine environments throughout the world from the lower to middle Cambrian.

evidence.title: Megacheira
evidence.text: The group might also contain one species ("Enalikter aphson") described from the Silurian Herefordshire Lagerstätte of the United Kingdom, and one species ("Bundenbachiellus giganteus") known from the Early Devonian of Germany; however, the interpretation of these taxa as megacheirans was challenged by Struck "et al." (2015).

evidence.title: Megacheira
evidence.text: Megacheirans were important components of several faunas, including the Burgess, Wheeler and Maotianshan Shales Lagerstatten.

evidence.title: Megacheira
evidence.text: Genera referred to the class include "Leanchoilia", "Alalcomenaeus", "Oestokerkus", "Yohoia", "Fortiforceps" and "Jianfengia".

evidence.title: Oligoryzomys fulvescens
evidence.text: Oligoryzomys fulvescens, also known as the fulvous colilargo, fulvous pygmy rice rat, or northern pygmy rice rat, is a species of rodent in the genus "Oligoryzomys" of family Cricetidae.

evidence.title: Oligoryzomys fulvescens
evidence.text: It is found from southern Mexico through Central America into South America, where it occurs south into Peru and Brazil, and includes numerous synonyms, including the type species of the genus, "Oryzomys navus" Bangs, 1899.

evidence.title: Oligoryzomys fulvescens
evidence.text: The taxonomy of this species is unresolved, and it may be found to contain more than one species.

evidence.title: Oligoryzomys fulvescens
evidence.text: Its karyotype has 2n = 54-60 and FNa = 68-74.

evidence.title: Cunninghamia
evidence.text: Cunninghamia is a genus of one or two living species of evergreen coniferous trees in the cypress family Cupressaceae.

evidence.title: Cunninghamia
evidence.text: They are native to China, northern Vietnam and Laos, and perhaps also Cambodia.

evidence.title: Cunninghamia
evidence.text: They may reach 50 m in height.

evidence.title: Cunninghamia
evidence.text: In vernacular use, it is most often known as "Cunninghamia", but is also sometimes called "China-fir" (though it is not a fir).

evidence.title: Cunninghamia
evidence.text: The genus name "Cunninghamia" honours Dr. James Cunningham, a British doctor who introduced this species into cultivation in 1702 and botanist Allan Cunningham.

evidence.title: Bupleurum
evidence.text: Bupleurum is a large genus of annual or perennial herbs or woody shrubs, with about one hundred and ninety species, belonging to the Apiaceae family.

evidence.title: Bupleurum
evidence.text: The full size of its species may vary between a few cm to up to 3 m high.

evidence.title: Bupleurum
evidence.text: Their compound umbels of small flowers are adorned with bracteoles that are sometimes large and may play a role in attracting pollinators.

evidence.title: Bupleurum
evidence.text: Rare among Apiaceae are the simple leaves, bracts (if present) and bracteoles.

evidence.title: Bupleurum
evidence.text: The genus is almost exclusively native in the Old World Northern Hemisphere, with one species native to North America and one species native to southern Africa.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: Anthocharis is a Holarctic genus of the butterfly tribe Anthocharini, in the Pieridae family.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: These are typically small, white-hued butterflies that have colorful marks just inside the tips of the forewings.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: The tip colors are usually a red-orange hue, hence the name "orange tip".

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: The larvae of these butterfly often consume cruciferous plants containing chemicals called glucosinolates.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: This genus is characterized by two of the five subcostal veins branching off before the apex of the cell, by the upper radial being only little united with the subcostal, and by the central discocellular being rather long.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: In all the species the males have at least the apical portion of the forewing orange red or yellow.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: Only one species inhabits also the northern districts of the Palearctic region, all the others are found in the south of the Palearctic region, also some species occur in North America, but not one species extends into the tropics.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: The Anthocharis species have only one brood.

evidence.title: Anthocharis
evidence.text: The butterflies occur in spring.

evidence.title: Chilopsis
evidence.text: Chilopsis is a monotypic genus of flowering plants containing the single species Chilopsis linearis.

evidence.title: Giraffe
evidence.text: The giraffe ("Giraffa") is a genus of African even-toed ungulate mammals, the tallest living terrestrial animals and the largest ruminants.

evidence.title: Giraffe
evidence.text: The genus currently consists of one species, "Giraffa camelopardalis", the type species.

evidence.title: Giraffe
evidence.text: Seven other species are extinct, prehistoric species known from fossils.

evidence.title: Giraffe
evidence.text: Taxonomic classifications of one to eight extant giraffe species have been described, based upon research into the mitochondrial and nuclear DNA, as well as morphological measurements of "Giraffa," but the IUCN currently recognizes only one species with nine subspecies.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: Argyrochosma is a genus of ferns known commonly as false cloak ferns.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: The genus is included in the Cheilanthoideae subfamily of the Pteridaceae.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: Species now in this genus were previously treated as members of related genera "Notholaena" or "Pellaea" but were segregated into their own genus in 1987.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: These ferns, of which there are about 20 species, are mostly native to the Americas, from North to South and including the Caribbean, while one species, "A. connectens", is known from Sichuan, China.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: They are commonly found growing in cracks between rocks.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: Their leaves are generally shorter than 40 centimeters and have rounded bluish or grayish green segments.

evidence.title: Argyrochosma
evidence.text: Often the lower surface of the segments is coated in a white dust, and the sporangia contain brown spores.
